location.name: Valley of Flowers National Park — Uttarakhand

questions.question: The Valley of Flowers is famous for its seasonal blooms during which period?
The valley was 'discovered' by a European mountaineering party in which year, after they lost their way?
The Valley of Flowers is part of which larger UNESCO-listed biosphere complex, alongside Nanda Devi National Park?
The valley is home to over 300 species of what?
The park closes to visitors for most of the year mainly due to what?

pins.summary: The Valley of Flowers, high in the Uttarakhand Himalayas, bursts into a riot of alpine blooms each monsoon, hosting over 300 species of flowering plants across its glacial valley floor. It was brought to wider attention in 1931 when British mountaineer Frank Smythe, descending from a peak, stumbled upon it and later wrote a book that gave the valley its enduring name. Accessible only for a few months each year due to heavy snow the rest of the time, it forms part of the Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005.

questions.question: The Marble Rocks at Bhedaghat form dramatic gorges along which river?
The gorge is famous for cliffs made of which type of rock, despite its name?
A popular way to view the Marble Rocks gorge is via what?
Bhedaghat is located near which major Madhya Pradesh city?
The nearby Dhuandhar Falls, meaning 'smoke cascade,' forms on the same river where it does what?
options: Plunges over the marble rocks creating misty spray

pins.summary: The Marble Rocks at Bhedaghat, near Jabalpur, are towering cliffs of pale magnesian limestone that the Narmada River has carved into a dramatic, narrow gorge over millennia. Despite the name, the rock is not true marble, but its smooth, pale surfaces glow strikingly white under moonlight, making moonlit boat rides a particular local attraction. Just upstream, the Narmada plunges roughly 15 metres over the Dhuandhar Falls — literally 'smoke cascade' — where the sheer force of the water throws up a constant mist resembling smoke, best viewed from cable-car platforms installed above the falls.

questions.question: Zanskar Valley is one of the most remote inhabited regions in which Union Territory?
Zanskar is famous for the frozen-river trekking route known as what, used historically to travel when roads were snowbound?
The Chadar Trek involves walking on the frozen surface of which river?
For several months each winter, Zanskar Valley is typically cut off from the rest of Ladakh due to what?
options: Heavy snow blocking the only motorable pass

questions.question: Zanskar's population is predominantly of which religious and cultural tradition?

pins.summary: Zanskar Valley, tucked deep in Ladakh's mountains, remains cut off from the rest of the region for much of winter, when the only motorable pass closes under heavy snow. For centuries, locals relied on the Chadar Trek — walking directly across the frozen Zanskar River — as their sole winter route to the outside world, a practice that has since also become a demanding, sought-after adventure trek for outsiders. Predominantly Tibetan Buddhist, Zanskar's isolated monasteries and villages have preserved a way of life and religious tradition little changed for generations, drawing travellers seeking Ladakh's most untouched corner.

location.name: Great Himalayan National Park — Himachal Pradesh

questions.question: The Great Himalayan National Park is located in which Himachal Pradesh district?
The park was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in which year?
The park protects habitat for which endangered high-altitude animal, among others?
The park's ecosystem spans an unusually wide altitude range, from river valleys up to what?
Local communities living near the park traditionally depended on it for which resource before conservation restrictions?

pins.summary: The Great Himalayan National Park in Himachal Pradesh's Kullu district protects an extraordinary altitude range — from temperate river valleys to alpine peaks nearing 6,000 metres — sheltering snow leopards, Himalayan tahr, and hundreds of bird species within a single contiguous ecosystem. Local Himalayan communities historically depended on the park's forests and high pastures for grazing livestock and gathering medicinal herbs, a relationship the park's management now tries to balance with strict conservation goals. UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site in 2014, citing its exceptional biodiversity across such compressed but dramatic terrain.

questions.question: Kanha National Park is believed to have inspired the setting of which famous literary work?
Kanha played a critical role in saving which endangered deer species from near-extinction?
Kanha National Park is located in which Indian state?
Kanha is one of India's designated reserves under which major tiger conservation programme, launched in 1973?
Rudyard Kipling, whose work is linked to Kanha's landscape, actually wrote it primarily set in which broader Indian forest region?
options: Central Indian forests (Seoni area, near Kanha)

pins.summary: Kanha National Park in Madhya Pradesh's dense sal and bamboo forests is widely believed to have inspired the setting of Rudyard Kipling's The Jungle Book, drawing on the wider Seoni forest region nearby. Beyond its literary fame, Kanha holds a genuine conservation milestone: it brought the barasingha, or swamp deer, back from the brink of extinction through decades of dedicated habitat management, growing the population from a few dozen to several hundred. One of the original nine reserves designated under Project Tiger in 1973, Kanha remains among India's most successful tiger conservation landscapes.

questions.question: Amer Fort (Amber Fort) overlooks which lake near Jaipur?
Amer Fort was the capital of which Rajput kingdom before Jaipur city was founded?
Amer Fort's most famous interior hall, decorated with intricate mirror-work, is called what?
Amer Fort was primarily constructed starting in which century, under Raja Man Singh I?
Amer Fort is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site listing that groups it with which other Rajasthani forts?

pins.summary: Amer Fort, perched above Maota Lake just outside Jaipur, served as the capital of the Kachwaha Rajput rulers before Jaipur city itself was founded in the 18th century. Built predominantly from the late 16th century under Raja Man Singh I, its blend of Rajput and Mughal architectural styles reaches a peak in the Sheesh Mahal, a hall whose walls and ceilings are inlaid with thousands of tiny mirrors that once turned a single candle's flame into a starlit sky. Amer Fort is part of the collective UNESCO World Heritage listing 'Hill Forts of Rajasthan,' recognised in 2013.

questions.question: Charminar was built in which year to commemorate the end of a plague epidemic, according to popular tradition?
Charminar was commissioned by which Qutb Shahi ruler?
'Charminar' literally translates to what in Urdu/Persian?
Charminar sits at the heart of Hyderabad's old city, historically at the centre of a bustling market known as what?
Charminar has a small mosque located on which level of the structure?

pins.summary: Charminar, built in 1591 by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, stands at the historic heart of Hyderabad's old city — its name literally meaning 'four minarets,' referring to the four towering, ornately carved spires anchoring each corner of the structure. Popular tradition holds it was built to mark the end of a devastating plague, though its exact founding rationale remains debated among historians. A small mosque occupies its upper floor, still in active use, while the surrounding streets host Laad Bazaar, a centuries-old market famous for bangles, pearls, and Hyderabadi perfumes, keeping Charminar a living commercial hub rather than a purely historical relic.

questions.question: Humayun's Tomb was commissioned by whom, in memory of Emperor Humayun?
Humayun's Tomb is often cited as an important architectural precursor to which more famous Mughal monument?
Humayun's Tomb was among the first Mughal structures in India to prominently use which building material?
options: Red sandstone with white marble accents

questions.question: The tomb complex is laid out in the classic Persian garden style known as what?
In 1857, Humayun's Tomb briefly served as a hiding place and later capture site for which historical figure?
options: The last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar

pins.summary: Humayun's Tomb, commissioned around 1565 by Empress Bega Begum for her late husband, is widely regarded as the architectural blueprint that eventually inspired the Taj Mahal, pioneering the use of red sandstone with white marble inlay and a formal charbagh garden layout in Mughal India. In 1857, during the Indian Rebellion, the tomb became a dramatic historical footnote when the last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, took refuge here before being captured by British forces, effectively ending Mughal rule. Restored extensively in recent decades, the complex is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and remains one of Delhi's most serene Mughal-era landmarks.

questions.question: Brihadeeswarar Temple was built by which Chola king in the 11th century?
The temple's massive central tower (vimana) rises to approximately what height, remarkable for its era?
The huge capstone atop the temple's tower is carved from a single block of what?
Brihadeeswarar Temple is dedicated to which deity?
The temple is part of a UNESCO World Heritage grouping called what, alongside two other Chola-era temples?

pins.summary: Brihadeeswarar Temple in Thanjavur, completed around 1010 CE under the Chola emperor Rajaraja I, is an engineering marvel of its age — its central tower rises some 66 metres, capped by a single 80-tonne granite block that ancient builders are believed to have hauled into place using a long earthen ramp, since cranes obviously didn't exist. Dedicated to Shiva, the temple showcases the peak of Chola architectural and artistic achievement, its walls covered in inscriptions and frescoes documenting the dynasty's administration and patronage. Along with two related Chola temples, it forms the UNESCO-listed 'Great Living Chola Temples,' still active places of daily worship after a thousand years.

questions.question: Qutub Minar was begun by which ruler, founder of the Delhi Sultanate's Mamluk dynasty?
Qutub Minar, at completion, became the tallest brick minaret of its kind, standing at approximately what height?
The famous Iron Pillar standing in the Qutub complex is renowned for its resistance to what?
Qutub Minar has how many distinct storeys, each marked by a projecting balcony?
The Qutub complex also contains the incomplete remains of what, intended to be an even taller rival tower?

pins.summary: Qutub Minar, begun around 1192 by Qutb-ud-din Aibak to mark the start of Muslim rule in Delhi, rises through five distinct storeys to about 73 metres, making it the tallest brick minaret in the world at the time of its construction. Within the same complex stands the enigmatic Iron Pillar, over 1,600 years old and remarkably rust-resistant, a metallurgical puzzle that continues to intrigue scientists. Sultan Alauddin Khalji later began an even more ambitious tower, the Alai Minar, intending to double Qutub Minar's height — but it was abandoned after reaching only about 25 metres and stands today as a stunted, unfinished stump beside its far more famous neighbour.

questions.question: Bhilai Steel Plant was established with technical collaboration from which country?
Bhilai Steel Plant is operated under which public sector company?
Bhilai Steel Plant became particularly renowned for producing which specific product used in India's space programme?
options: Rails for railway tracks and specialised steel for ISRO

questions.question: Bhilai Steel Plant's establishment in the 1950s was part of India's push toward what economic model?
options: State-led industrialisation under the Second Five-Year Plan

questions.question: Bhilai is one of several major steel plants set up in India during the same era with foreign collaboration; which country helped set up the Rourkela plant?

pins.summary: Bhilai Steel Plant in Chhattisgarh, established with Soviet technical collaboration and commissioned in 1959, was a flagship project of India's early state-led industrialisation drive under the Second Five-Year Plan. Operated today by the Steel Authority of India (SAIL), Bhilai became particularly known for manufacturing the specialised rails that carry much of India's rail network, as well as high-grade steel components supplied to ISRO's space programme. Alongside contemporaries like Rourkela (built with West German help) and Durgapur (British collaboration), Bhilai exemplified the Nehruvian era's strategy of building heavy industry through partnerships with different global powers simultaneously.

questions.question: Kandla Port was developed in the years following independence primarily to replace which port lost to Pakistan at Partition?
Kandla was renamed Deendayal Port in which year?
Kandla Port is located on which gulf on India's western coast?
Kandla was India's first port to be declared what type of trade zone in 1965?
options: Special Economic Zone under current terminology

questions.question: Kandla Port primarily handles which major category of cargo?
options: Bulk cargo including petroleum, chemicals and food grains

pins.summary: Kandla Port, on Gujarat's Gulf of Kutch coastline, was developed in the years after Partition specifically to compensate for the loss of Karachi, which had handled much of undivided India's western maritime trade. In 1965, Kandla became India's first Export Processing Zone, an early precursor to today's Special Economic Zones, aimed at boosting industrial exports. Renamed Deendayal Port in 2017, it remains one of India's busiest ports by cargo volume, handling substantial bulk trade in petroleum products, chemicals, and food grains for the country's northern and western hinterlands.

questions.question: Hinjewadi IT Park, on the outskirts of Pune, is a major hub for which industry?
Hinjewadi is officially developed and managed as part of which government-backed initiative?
options: Software Technology Parks of India (STPI) / Rajiv Gandhi Infotech Park

questions.question: Pune, where Hinjewadi is located, is often nicknamed what, reflecting its educational and industrial importance?
Hinjewadi hosts offices of numerous major IT and consulting firms, contributing significantly to which state's IT exports?
A recurring civic challenge associated with Hinjewadi's rapid IT-driven growth has been what?
options: Severe traffic congestion and inadequate public transport

pins.summary: Hinjewadi IT Park, part of the Rajiv Gandhi Infotech Park initiative on Pune's western outskirts, has grown into one of Maharashtra's largest information technology employment hubs, hosting offices of major global IT and consulting firms. Pune, sometimes called the 'Oxford of the East' for its dense concentration of colleges and universities, has leveraged this educated talent pool to build a substantial software services economy alongside its older identity as an automobile and manufacturing centre. Hinjewadi's explosive, largely unplanned growth has also made it a case study in urban infrastructure strain, with chronic traffic congestion prompting ongoing metro and road expansion projects.

questions.question: Dadri serves as a key terminal node for which major Indian rail infrastructure project?
The Dedicated Freight Corridor project was primarily designed to separate what from congested passenger rail lines?
Dadri's location makes it an important logistics link for goods moving between Delhi-NCR and which direction?
Dedicated Freight Corridors in India were primarily developed to reduce reliance on which more polluting/costly mode of long-haul cargo transport?
The Eastern Dedicated Freight Corridor primarily connects Dadri (near Delhi) to which eastern terminus?

pins.summary: The freight terminal at Dadri, on Delhi's eastern fringe, anchors the western end of India's Eastern Dedicated Freight Corridor, a purpose-built rail line running roughly 1,300 km to Dankuni near Kolkata, designed exclusively for goods trains. By separating freight from the country's overloaded passenger rail network, the corridor allows longer, heavier trains to move faster and more reliably, easing pressure on both older rail lines and India's congested highways, which had long carried a disproportionate share of long-haul freight by truck. Dadri's role as a key logistics node has grown alongside Delhi-NCR's expansion as a major consumption and distribution hub for northern India.

questions.question: NTPC Vindhyachal is one of India's largest what type of power stations?
NTPC, which operates Vindhyachal, stands for what?
NTPC Vindhyachal is situated in which Madhya Pradesh district?
The Singrauli region, home to Vindhyachal, is often referred to informally as India's what, due to its dense concentration of coal-based power plants?
NTPC Vindhyachal's massive coal consumption raises ongoing concerns primarily related to what?

pins.summary: NTPC Vindhyachal, located in Madhya Pradesh's coal-rich Singrauli district, is among the largest coal-based thermal power stations operated by NTPC (National Thermal Power Corporation), India's largest power utility. Singrauli's dense cluster of thermal plants, drawing on nearby coalfields, has earned the region an informal reputation as one of India's key energy hubs, supplying electricity to a wide swath of northern and central India. That same concentration of coal-fired generation has also made Singrauli a focal point in India's ongoing debates over balancing energy security and industrial growth against air quality and climate concerns.

questions.question: Ganesh Chaturthi celebrates the birth of which deity?
The festival's public, community-organised celebrations in Maharashtra were popularised on a large scale by which freedom-movement leader?
Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations traditionally conclude with a ritual immersion of idols called what?
Mumbai's most famous and heavily visited Ganesh pandal, drawing massive crowds annually, is popularly known as what?
Tilak's promotion of public Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations in the 1890s was strategically aimed at doing what, under colonial rule?
options: Uniting people across caste lines against British restrictions on gatherings

pins.summary: Ganesh Chaturthi, honouring the birth of Lord Ganesha, became a mass public festival largely through the efforts of freedom-movement leader Bal Gangadhar Tilak, who in the 1890s promoted community-organised celebrations as a clever way to unite Indians across caste and class lines at a time when the British colonial administration restricted large political gatherings. Mumbai's ten-day festival today culminates in the visarjan, when enormous, elaborately decorated idols are carried in processions to the sea for ritual immersion — none more anticipated than Lalbaugcha Raja, whose pandal draws millions of devotees and hours-long queues each year.

questions.question: Karva Chauth is a fasting ritual traditionally observed by married women for whose long life and wellbeing?
The Karva Chauth fast is traditionally broken only after sighting which celestial body in the evening?
Karva Chauth is most strongly associated with which regions of India historically?
options: North India, especially Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and UP

questions.question: The word 'Karva' in Karva Chauth refers to what ritual object commonly used during the festival?
In recent decades, Karva Chauth traditions have also increasingly been adopted by whom, beyond the original custom?
options: Unmarried women and sometimes husbands reciprocally fasting
Only among a single religious community

pins.summary: Karva Chauth, observed predominantly across Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, and parts of Uttar Pradesh, sees married women undertake a rigorous day-long fast — often without even water — for the long life and wellbeing of their husbands, breaking the fast only after sighting the moon through a decorative sieve, often illuminated further by the glow of a diya. The 'karva' refers to the small earthen pot used in the associated rituals and gift exchanges. While traditionally a women-only observance, the custom has evolved in recent decades, with growing numbers of husbands choosing to reciprocally fast, and unmarried women in some communities now participating too, reflecting the festival's gradual shift from strict tradition toward a broader, more mutual expression of devotion.

questions.question: Poila Boishakh marks the first day of which regional calendar's new year?
Poila Boishakh typically falls in which month of the Gregorian calendar?
A traditional business practice on Poila Boishakh in Bengal involves shopkeepers opening a new what?
Poila Boishakh celebrations in Kolkata often include cultural processions inspired by which broader Indian tradition of welcoming the new year with art?
options: Mangal Shobhajatra-style processions with masks and folk art

questions.question: Poila Boishakh is celebrated by Bengali communities in which neighbouring country as well, where it is also a major national holiday?

pins.summary: Poila Boishakh, the Bengali New Year, falls in mid-April and is celebrated with equal enthusiasm in Kolkata and across the border in Bangladesh, where it is a major national holiday. Traditionally, Bengali shopkeepers mark the day by opening a fresh account ledger, the Haal Khata, closing out old debts and starting the new business year with sweets and goodwill toward customers. Kolkata's celebrations increasingly feature colourful cultural processions drawing on folk art and mask traditions, while families gather for elaborate Bengali feasts, new clothes, and visits to Kali temples to seek blessings for the year ahead.

questions.question: Gudi Padwa marks the traditional New Year in which state?
The festival's name comes from the 'gudi,' a decorated pole displayed outside homes, symbolising what?
Gudi Padwa falls on the same lunar calendar date associated with which other well-known regional new year festival?
options: Ugadi (celebrated in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka)

questions.question: According to popular belief, Gudi Padwa also commemorates a legendary victory associated with which historical/mythological figure?
options: Lord Rama's return to Ayodhya, or the start of the Shalivahana calendar era

questions.question: A distinctive sweet-and-bitter dish traditionally eaten on Gudi Padwa, symbolising life's mixed experiences, is made using neem leaves and what?

pins.summary: Gudi Padwa marks the traditional New Year in Maharashtra, falling on the same lunar date as Ugadi further south, and is heralded by hoisting a gudi — a bamboo pole decked with a bright cloth, neem leaves, and an upturned copper or silver vessel — outside homes, symbolising victory and prosperity. According to tradition, the day also commemorates the legendary start of the Shalivahana calendar era and, in some retellings, Lord Rama's triumphant return to Ayodhya. Maharashtrian households mark the day with a distinctive dish combining neem leaves and jaggery, a deliberate mix of bitter and sweet meant to symbolise accepting both hardship and joy as the year unfolds.

questions.question: Eid-ul-Fitr marks the end of which Islamic observance?
Lucknow, a major centre for Eid celebrations in North India, is historically associated with which former ruling dynasty known for its refined culture?
A mandatory act of charity that Muslims are expected to perform before Eid-ul-Fitr prayers is called what?
Lucknow's Eid festivities are famous for which culinary tradition, reflecting its Nawabi heritage?
Eid-ul-Fitr celebrations begin with special congregational prayers held typically at which time of day?

pins.summary: Eid-ul-Fitr, celebrated in Lucknow with particular grandeur reflecting the city's Nawabi heritage, marks the joyful end of Ramadan's month-long fasting. Before the morning's congregational prayers, Muslims are expected to give zakat al-Fitr, a charitable donation ensuring less fortunate community members can also join in the celebrations. Lucknow's Eid tables are renowned for their elaborate spread — rich sheer khurma (a vermicelli milk dessert), slow-cooked kebabs, and biryanis — culinary traditions refined over centuries under the Nawabs of Awadh, whose courtly emphasis on hospitality and refined taste still shapes the city's festive food culture today.

questions.question: Delhi's official constitutional status is best described as what?
options: A National Capital Territory (NCT) with partial statehood powers
A Union Territory with no legislature

questions.question: Delhi's special status as NCT was created through which constitutional amendment?
Unlike full states, Delhi's elected government has historically had limited or contested control over which key areas?
Delhi's head of administration appointed by the Central Government is known as what?
Disputes over the division of power between Delhi's elected government and the Lieutenant Governor have frequently gone to which body for resolution?

pins.summary: Delhi occupies a unique constitutional position as a National Capital Territory, a status created by the 69th Constitutional Amendment in 1991 that granted it its own elected Legislative Assembly and Chief Minister, while still falling short of full statehood. Critical subjects like police, public order, and land remain under the control of the Lieutenant Governor, representing the Central Government, a division of power that has repeatedly sparked friction between Delhi's elected government and the Centre. These recurring disputes over jurisdiction have on several occasions reached the Supreme Court, which has issued rulings attempting to clarify the boundaries of authority between the two.

questions.question: Article 371A grants special constitutional provisions to which state?
Under Article 371A, Parliament generally cannot legislate on Naga religious and social practices without the consent of what?
Article 371A also provides special protection concerning Naga customary law and which specific resource?
Article 371A was incorporated into the Constitution following an agreement made in which year, paving the way for Nagaland's statehood?
Nagaland became a full-fledged state of India in which year?

pins.summary: Article 371A, incorporated as part of a 1960 agreement that paved the way for Nagaland's statehood in 1963, grants the state distinctive constitutional protections not extended to most other Indian states. It ensures Parliament cannot legislate on matters of Naga religious or social practice, customary law, or ownership and transfer of land and its resources without the concurrence of the Nagaland Legislative Assembly. These provisions reflect the unique historical negotiations around Naga identity and self-governance that shaped the state's entry into the Indian Union, and they remain a frequently cited reference point in ongoing discussions about autonomy across India's northeastern states.

questions.question: India's modern Panchayati Raj system of local self-governance was first formally launched in which state, at Nagaur district, in 1959?
The committee whose recommendations led to the creation of the Panchayati Raj system was headed by whom?
Panchayati Raj institutions were given firm constitutional status through which amendment, passed in 1992?
The Panchayati Raj system operates through a three-tier structure: Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti, and which third tier?
Which Prime Minister formally inaugurated the first Panchayati Raj institution at Nagaur in 1959?

pins.summary: India's modern Panchayati Raj system of village self-governance traces its formal origin to Nagaur district in Rajasthan, where Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru inaugurated the first such institution in October 1959, based on recommendations from a committee headed by Balwant Rai Mehta. The system envisioned a three-tier structure of local democracy — Gram Panchayats at the village level, Panchayat Samitis at the block level, and Zila Parishads at the district level — designed to decentralise development planning and give rural communities direct say in local governance. It took over three decades, however, for Panchayati Raj to gain firm constitutional backing, achieved through the 73rd Amendment in 1992, which made such elected local bodies mandatory across rural India.

questions.question: The Election Commission of India is a constitutional body responsible for overseeing elections to which offices?
options: Parliament, state legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President

questions.question: The Election Commission was originally established as a single-member body; when did it become a multi-member commission?
The head of the Election Commission of India holds the title of what?
The Election Commission derives its authority primarily from which article of the Indian Constitution?
A key tool the Election Commission uses to ensure fair conduct during elections, restricting government announcements and campaigning, is called what?

pins.summary: The Election Commission of India, established under Article 324 of the Constitution, is the autonomous body responsible for administering elections to Parliament, state legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President. Originally a single-member body since its founding in 1950, it became a multi-member commission during 1989-1993, adding a Chief Election Commissioner and two additional Election Commissioners to strengthen institutional checks. Among its most significant tools is the Model Code of Conduct, a set of guidelines that restricts government announcements, spending, and campaign conduct once elections are announced, intended to ensure a level playing field — though its enforcement and scope remain a frequent subject of political debate.

location.name: Comptroller and Auditor General of India — Delhi

questions.question: The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India is primarily responsible for auditing what?
options: The accounts and expenditure of the Union and state governments

questions.question: The CAG is often described using which phrase, emphasising its role in financial accountability?
The CAG's reports on government spending are submitted to whom for further parliamentary scrutiny?
options: The Prime Minister directly, with no further review
The President, and then examined by the Public Accounts Committee

questions.question: The office of the CAG derives its constitutional basis from which article?
The CAG is appointed by whom, and holds office for how long or until what age limit?
options: The Prime Minister; 5 years or age 65
The President; 6 years or age 65, whichever is earlier
The Parliament by direct vote; 10 years

pins.summary: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India, established under Article 148 of the Constitution, functions as the guardian of the public purse, auditing the financial accounts and expenditure of both the Union and state governments to ensure public money is spent as authorised by Parliament and state legislatures. Appointed by the President for a term of six years or until age 65, whichever comes first, the CAG submits audit reports that are placed before Parliament and then scrutinised in detail by the Public Accounts Committee. Over the decades, several high-profile CAG reports on issues like telecom spectrum allocation and coal block distribution have triggered major political controversies, underscoring the office's significant, if sometimes contested, role in India's system of financial accountability.
